Consequently, the bound becomes small at long offsets, explaining the weak average Euclidean cost signal for distinguishing states which are distant to goal in Fig. 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Changes in the components of Euclidean temporal contrast on AntMaze (left) and FourRoom (right), using 50 recorded planner executions per environment. The horizontal axis is the separation $k$ from a sampled future goal in model steps, with a fixed comparison gap of $\Delta=1$ model step (five environment steps). Curves show $|\delta_{\Delta}B(k)|$ and $|\delta_{\Delta}q(k)|$, each divided by the environment’s mean Euclidean squared distance $\overline{D}_{E}$ over the tested offsets. In both environments, the $B$ term varies little, while changes in the $q$ term become smaller at longer offsets.
figures.headline: In AntMaze and FourRoom, the mean-difference term changes little, while the cross-covariance term changes less at longer offsets.
citing_sentences: Empirically, Fig. 2 shows this behavior on 50 recorded planner executions each in AntMaze and FourRoom.
These observations agree with the component analysis in Fig. 2, which links weak Euclidean contrast to small changes in $B(k)$ and $q(k)$.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview of T2G metric training. A latent triple $({\bf z}_{t},{\bf z}_{t+k},{\bf z}_{t+k+\Delta})$ is sampled from an offline trajectory, where the near and far states are separated from the anchor by $k$ and $k+\Delta$ steps, respectively. The three encoder blocks denote the same frozen JEPA encoder applied to the corresponding observations. T2G evaluates the learned temporal distances from the anchor to the near and far latents and optimizes the metric with a margin ranking objective, so that the near state is closer to the anchor than the far state by at least a margin $m$. Only the metric network and its scale are updated, and the world model remains frozen.
figures.headline: T2G training samples anchor, near and far latent states from offline clips and updates only the metric network and its scale.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Overview of T2G planning. The current observation $o_{1}$ and goal observation $o_{g}$ are encoded into latents ${\bf z}_{1}$ and ${\bf z}_{g}$ by the frozen JEPA encoder. A solver optimizes an action sequence $a_{1:H}$, and the frozen predictor rolls out the resulting latent trajectory ${\bf z}_{1}\!\to\!{\bf z}_{2}\!\to\!\cdots\!\to\!{\bf z}_{H}$. Each predicted latent is scored by its learned temporal distance to the goal, $d_{\theta}({\bf z}_{t},{\bf z}_{g})$, and the solver updates the actions to minimize the aggregated cost. The updated actions are executed and planning is repeated from new observations in a receding-horizon loop, while the encoder, predictor, and solver remain unchanged.
figures.headline: Planning scores each predicted latent by its learned distance to the goal while the encoder, predictor and solver stay unchanged.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Temporal guidance of Euclidean squared and T2G costs on recorded AntMaze (top) and FourRoom (bottom) executions. Left: mean cost to the same sampled future goals, normalized by each cost’s mean over the tested offsets. Middle: normalized temporal contrast between offsets separated by one model step (five environment steps). Right: the fraction of comparisons in which the temporally nearer state receives a lower cost, with ties receiving half credit; the dashed line marks 50%. Horizontal axes report temporal separation in environment steps. At long offsets, T2G maintains a larger positive contrast and higher ranking accuracy in both environments.

citing_sentences: To examine the temporal guidance discussed in Section 2.2, Fig. 6 compares Euclidean squared and T2G costs on 50 recorded executions per environment from flat LeWM with T2G last-$2$.

abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near–far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7% (flat LeWM) to 63.0% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model. Code is available at https://github.com/yrluestc/T2G-JEPA.

sections.body: JEPAs predict future latent states and plan by comparing predicted states with an encoded goal. LeWM trains its encoder and predictor with a next-embedding loss and a SIGReg regularizer, and its planner uses Euclidean distance to the goal. The section argues that a flat planner may give an unreliable progress signal over long horizons, and that a distant goal can be hard to match. H-JEPA addresses this with a hierarchy, but it changes both prediction and evaluation, so its gains mix architectural and cost effects. The authors therefore isolate the goal cost and propose T2G, a learned temporal metric with 0.182M parameters, 1.6% of flat LeWM. T2G changes the cost while the world model stays unchanged.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Flat JEPA planners with Euclidean goal costs give unreliable progress signals over long horizons, motivating a better cost alone.

sections.body: The section decomposes the mean squared Euclidean distance between a state at offset $k$ and a future goal into $B(k)$ minus twice $q(k)$, where $B(k)$ holds the squared mean difference and marginal variance traces, and $q(k)$ is the cross-covariance trace. The temporal contrast between offsets $k$ and $k+1$ is bounded by changes in these terms. On 50 recorded executions per environment, the $B$ term varies little, while the $q$ term changes less at longer offsets, so the bound becomes small. T2G applies a scaled distance, with a learned scale, to a small network's outputs on frozen latents. It is trained on anchor, near and far triples from offline clips with a margin ranking loss, using no rewards or policy labels.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Euclidean contrast shrinks at long offsets, so T2G learns a margin-ranked distance over latent triples from offline trajectories.

sections.body: Evaluation covers FourRoomDistractors, Visual AntMaze, Push-T and OGBench Cube, with 50 start-goal tasks per environment and success measured over seeds 42, 43 and 44. Flat LeWM reaches 18.0% on AntMaze, 32.0% on Cube, 40.7% on FourRoom and 40.0% on Push-T. T2G last-n reaches 58.7%, 63.3%, 78.7% and 51.3% on these tasks. The averages are 63.0% for T2G last-n, 53.3%, 61.7% and 49.8% for two-, three- and four-level H-JEPA. Dense T2G drops Cube to 4.0%, which the authors attribute to penalizing intermediate grasp-preparation states. Three-level H-JEPA reaches 96.0% on FourRoom, higher than any T2G row.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: T2G last-n raises the four-benchmark average success rate from 32.7% to 63.0%, near or above hierarchical baselines.

sections.body: The section groups reward-free JEPA world models such as DINO-WM, PLDM, V-JEPA 2 and LeWM, which are usually paired with CEM or gradient-based planning. It contrasts these with reward-based models such as Dreamer, TD-MPC2 and MuZero. Hierarchical methods include options, HWM and H-JEPA, which predicts subgoals across timescales. Temporal progress has also been studied with time-contrastive objectives and goal-conditioned value functions, which usually learn a policy or value function and rely on interaction or reward. The authors state that T2G adds no hierarchy and changes no world model. It learns a metric from offline latents with a margin ranking objective and serves as a cost for flat planners.
sections.heading: Related Works
sections.headline: Related work separates T2G from hierarchical JEPA planners and from reward-based temporal learning methods.

sections.body: The conclusion states that the cost used to score predicted states plays an important role in latent planning. T2G uses trajectory order to shape this cost while the frozen predictive representation stays fixed. The comparison of dense and last-n costs shows that which predicted states are scored matters, because emphasizing final states allows intermediate actions needed to complete a task. The authors plan two extensions: learning temporal costs at multiple levels to combine T2G with hierarchical planning, and applying the metric to physical robots using offline robot trajectories. They note that such tests would examine real visual variation, sensor noise and contact dynamics, which the simulated benchmarks do not cover.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The goal cost strongly affects latent planning, and trajectory order can supply supervision that shapes it.

sections.body: Experiments ran on Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS with 256 GB of RAM and a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Triples are sampled by drawing a near offset, then a gap, clipping the far offset at the maximum offset, and drawing the anchor index so the far state stays inside the clip. The metric uses two hidden blocks of width 256 with LayerNorm and GELU, and a softplus-parameterized scale initialized to 1. Training uses AdamW with learning rate 5e-5, weight decay 1e-3, batch size 128, 5 epochs, margin m=1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Input dimension is 384 for AntMaze and 192 for the other environments. Table 3 gives image sizes, clip lengths and maximum offsets for each environment.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists hardware, the triple sampling procedure, training hyperparameters, and per-environment input and sampling settings.
